paragraphs: Scientific consensus is that humans first began to have a warming effect on Earth’s climate within the past century, after coal-burning factories, power plants, and motor vehicles began releasing carbon dioxide (CO ) and other greenhouse gases in significant quantities into the 2 air. However, evidence suggests that human agricultural activities may have had such an effect much earlier: concentrations of CO started rising about 8000 years ago, even 2 though natural trends indicate they should have been dropping; methane levels rose similarly about 3,000 years later. Without these rises, however, current temperatures in northern parts of North America and Europe would be cooler by three to four degrees Celsius-enough to inhibit agriculture-and an ice age would probably have begun several thousand years ago in northeastern Canada.

paragraphs: Princessfish are a species of coral-reef fish that are captured alive by divers who first stun the individual fish by squirting a certain poison at them. Since the divers limit their catch to a few individuals and take care not to overfish, the divers’ continuing activities will clearly not result in serious harm to populations of princessfish.

With few exceptions, the many commercial frozen foods introduced in the United States in the 1950s found little consumer acceptance, in part because few Americans had significant freezer space. Most freestanding freezers were owned by farm families, who tended to fill their freezers with their own produce. Meanwhile, the working couples and small families in cities and towns whom the food industry had identified as the likeliest consumers of commercial frozen food lacked freezer space. While new refrigerators coming on the market had large separate freezer compartments, many consumers still used old refrigerators with tiny interior freezer compartments, and such consumers seemed convinced that they did not have space for a freestanding freezer in a small house or apartment.

Archaeologists studying Bonito phase (ca. A.D. 900-1140) Native American ceramics from Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, observed that many pots had been altered after firing to revise their decorative designs--usually, intricate geometric patterns painted in black on white slipped surfaces. In some cases, a new design was imposed over an earlier one; less often, the original design was simply covered with white slip. Crown and Wills doubt that the alterations were made to correct design errors. Many Chaco pots with design errors were left unaltered. Furthermore, when errors were corrected, revisions were made prior to firing—either by painting directly over the error or by scraping off designs and applying new slip and paint, which is a less time-consuming method than repainting and refiring flawed pots.

Reasons for uncertainty about the timing of the Thule migration [the movement of a proto-Inuit culture from Alaska to northern Canada and Greenland] are many, but primary among them are the well-known problems with radiocarbon dating in the Arctic. In particular, radiocarbon dates obtained on two kinds of organic remains that typically are common in the remains of Thule dwellings—driftwood and sea mammal bone—are likely to be older than the archaeological context in which they are found. Driftwood found in archaeological sites in the form of fuel or as part of an artifact assemble age may have sat on beaches for centuries before being utilized, and sea mammal bone is subject to the marine reservoir effect in which living tissue (including bone) incorporates ancient carbon, which also results in dates that are too old. Beyond this, however, many dates obtained in decades past simply seem too old, and there is a widespread suspicion among archaeologists that pretreatment methods may not always have eliminated the presence of substances derived from sea mammals, especially fat, which can be absorbed into wood, bone, and other materials and thereby contaminate them. As a result of these and other factors, both McGhee and Park have shown that the full spectrum of existing Thule radiocarbon dates, numbering in the hundreds, covers much too wide a range to reflect Thule chronology accurately.
